target.title: Poster: Recognizing Hidden-in-the-Ear Private Key for Reliable Silent Speech Interface Using Multi-Task Learning
target.venue: Companion of the 2025 ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp Companion ’25), October 12–16, 2025, Espoo, Finland

entries.text: HEar-ID combines low-frequency whisper audio and ultrasonic ear-canal reflections from consumer ANC earbuds for spelling and authentication.
entries.condition: A shared encoder feeds contrastive authentication and silent-spelling heads.
entries.quote:
We present HEar-ID, which uses consumer active noise–canceling earbuds to capture low-frequency “whisper” audio and high-
frequency ultrasonic reflections.

entries.text: The authors claim HEar-ID is the first earable system to authenticate through silent or whispered speech.
entries.condition: Novelty claim is qualified by “to our knowledge”; no independent survey is supplied in this paper.
entries.quote: To our knowledge, HEar-ID is the first earable solution to authenticate via silent or whispered speech.

entries.text: CLWUM is presented as a contrastive private-key space aligning genuine-user whisper and ultrasonic embeddings while repelling mismatched samples.
entries.condition: The contrastive branch uses paired whisper and ultrasonic samples from genuine users.
entries.quote: CLWUM exploits this intrinsic link by mapping paired whisper and ultrasonic signals into a shared embedding space, effectively acting as a “private key” that aligns only genuine-user embeddings.

entries.text: The system is presented as spelling words and authenticating users with one model on commodity earbuds.
entries.condition: Word-level spelling; in the reported study users articulated the lexicon with subtle voice.
entries.quote: This design supports decoding of 50 words while reliably rejecting impostors, all on commodity earbuds with a single model.

entries.text: The two input streams are ultrasonic reflections at 17.5–23 kHz and whisper audio at 0–11 kHz.
entries.condition: Ultrasonic band is isolated with a high-pass filter; the original audio is low-pass filtered for whisper features.
entries.quote: ultrasonic waveforms (17.5–23kHz) and whispers (0-11kHz)

entries.text: The study used an Edifier W380NB ANC earbud modified by removing its in-ear microphone from the circuitry and wiring it to a Google Pixel 3a for raw audio.
entries.condition: Experimental capture setup; the paper does not test the unmodified retail audio path end-to-end.

entries.text: The emitted OFDM signal has 2,046 samples at a 48 kHz sampling rate and lasts about 42 ms.
entries.condition: Ultrasonic signal used for alignment and ear-canal reflection sensing.
entries.quote:
HEar-ID leverages an OFDM signal of 2046 samples over a sam-
pling rate of 48000Hz, lasting for about 42ms.

entries.text: Training minimizes a weighted sum of contrastive, authentication, and CTC losses with weights 0.1, 0.5, and 0.3, respectively.
entries.condition: The paper says weights were set after hyperparameter tuning; optimizer and epoch count are not reported.

entries.text: The contrastive loss temperature is set to 0.7 based on empirical experience.
entries.condition: CLWUM genuine-user whisper–ultrasonic cross-modal contrastive objective.

entries.text: The angular triplet margin is first stated as 11.45 and later as 30 degrees; the two reported values are inconsistent or under-explained.
entries.condition: Authentication angular triplet loss; the paper does not reconcile the two margin statements.

entries.text: The authentication threshold is calibrated using Youden’s J statistic, but its numeric value and calibration set are not given.
entries.condition: Paper specifies the calibration rule but not which samples or partition determine the threshold.
entries.quote: We calibrate the 𝑡ℎ𝑟 with Youden’s J statistics [34], and adopt the empirical value of m as 30 degrees.

entries.text: The spelling head predicts 26 letters plus a blank symbol and is trained with CTC against letter sequences without frame-wise labels.
entries.condition: Word spelling is represented as a target letter sequence; CTC aligns frame logits to that sequence.

entries.text: The concatenated embeddings produce frame-level letter logits decoded to a spelled word; beam search is mentioned only as an example.
entries.condition: Beam width, decoding configuration, and any language-model use are not specified.

entries.text: At use time, a user spells a word; access is accepted when similarity to at least one stored reference embedding exceeds the threshold, otherwise access is denied.
entries.condition: The spelling head concurrently decodes the word from concatenated whisper and ultrasonic embeddings.
entries.quote: If the similarity to at least one reference embedding exceeds the threshold, the user is accepted; otherwise, access is denied.

entries.text: Registration uses a small set of user spellings and trains with other individuals’ data as impostor examples; the authors suggest manufacturers could supply that extra data.
entries.condition: The registration set size is described only as small/few-shot; no exact count is reported.
entries.quote: We claim that these extra training data can be provided by the manufacturer along with the product.

entries.text: The experiment included 11 participants: 10 from a ReHEarSSE subset and one additional recruit; the cohort was 9 male and 2 female with mean age 22.
entries.unit: participants; participants; participant; males; females; years mean age
entries.condition: Preliminary study cohort for spelling and authentication.

entries.text: All participants spelled the same 50 randomly selected words from the 1,000 most-used Oxford English Dictionary words for four rounds, using subtle voice.
entries.condition: A fixed lexicon was repeated; fully voiceless speech and unseen-word generalization were not evaluated.
entries.quote: All participants spelled 4 rounds of the same lexicon of 50 randomly selected words from the 1000 most used words from the Oxford English Dictionary [27] with subtle voice

entries.text: For each participant, one randomly selected re-wearing session was test and all other sessions were training; the authentication head and CLWUM used all participants’ data, while spelling was user-dependent.
entries.condition: Session-held-out split within the same 11 speakers; this is not a held-out-speaker evaluation.
entries.quote: For each participant, we form the testing set by randomly choosing a re-wearing session, and the training set by all other sessions except the left-out session.

entries.text: Each participant’s model was tested against 500 impostor attempts and 50 genuine-user accesses.
entries.unit: impostor attacks; genuine accesses per participant model
entries.condition: Authentication testing across the reported participant cohort.

entries.text: The whisper-plus-ultrasonic SSI reports mean Top-1 word accuracy of 67.3% across the study.
entries.condition: 11 participants; fixed 50-word lexicon; session holdout; recognition model is user-dependent.
entries.quote: Our whisper + ultrasonic SSI attains a mean Top-1 accuracy of 67.3 %.

entries.text: For 8 of 11 users without degraded ultrasonic sensing, the authors report 90.25% Top-1 accuracy.
entries.condition: Subset described as users without degraded ultrasonic sensing; same 50-word lexicon and session-held-out experiment; exact subset membership is not listed.
entries.quote: we achieved 90.25% Top-1 accuracy, which is comparable to the ultrasonic-only ReHEarSSE baseline (91.4 %).

entries.condition: Comparison is for the reported subset and fixed lexicon; no statistical comparison is reported.

entries.text: The microphone captures vocal audio plus ultrasound reflected from skin around the mouth; filtering separates the streams, and cross-correlation of each FMCW echo frame produces an Echo Profile whose temporal difference represents mouth movement.
entries.condition: Echoic sensing uses emitted ultrasonic FMCW and microphone-recorded reflections; the vocal and echoic streams are processed by separate KWS models.

entries.text: The active-acoustic carrier is two simultaneous FMCW chirp bands, 17–20 kHz and 20.5–23.5 kHz, with a 12 ms period; audio is sampled at 48 kHz.

questions.q: Do the reported spelling and authentication results establish performance beyond the studied users and sessions?
questions.answer: No. The evaluation holds out a re-wearing session per participant but uses the same participants for training and testing authentication/CLWUM (t18, t33). The overall Top-1 mean is 67.3%, while 90.25% is limited to eight users without degraded ultrasonic sensing (t20, t21); S5, S9, and S10 have recognition below 10%, and S9/S10 have near-zero authentication TPR (t41, t42). No repeated seeded runs or confidence intervals are reported (t29, t36).

questions.q: Which reported authentication figures need clarification before quantitative comparison?
questions.answer: The paper reports mean TPR/FPR of 81.76%/3.2% (t24), while the 11 displayed per-user labels average to TPR 80.00% and FPR 3.27% by arithmetic (inference; t25, t26). S5's prose TPR of 99.9% also differs from its 98.00% figure label (t27). The text names EER as a metric but supplies no EER result (t46).
